methodological_rigor.justification: The manuscript uses a retrospective imaging dataset of 533 glioma patients with molecular labels and states that patient-level splitting was used, but the evaluation design is internally inconsistent: methods describe 80/10/10 training/validation/test sets, while results describe 80/20 testing and separate 10-fold cross-validation on the same combined cohort. It reports high classification metrics but provides no calibration, confidence intervals for model performance, prespecified primary endpoint, or independent institution-level external validation distinct from model development. The single selected axial T2 slice per patient reduces leakage risk but also limits reproducibility and may discard clinically relevant tumor heterogeneity.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: This is a retrospective diagnostic prediction-model study using preoperative T2-weighted MRI and molecular labels from resected tissue, so it fits low-level observational diagnostic evidence rather than a prospective clinical-impact study. The target is clinically meaningful because noninvasive prediction of IDH and 1p/19q status could reduce dependence on invasive tissue procedures, but the manuscript evaluates only algorithmic accuracy and not treatment decisions, outcomes, workflow impact, or prospective reader performance. The reported sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy support plausibility, but clinical utility remains unproven.

reporting_quality.justification: TRIPOD is the closest standard because the manuscript develops and evaluates a prediction model, but key items are weakly reported, including outcome definition details, missing-data handling, model calibration, sample-size justification, and a coherent validation strategy. The text gives some dataset composition, preprocessing, split strategy, metrics, and hardware, yet the abstract, methods, and results conflict about test-set and cross-validation procedures. No usable data repository, trained model, code, or reproducible analysis package is described in the normalized manuscript.

novelty_literature.justification: The main novelty is methodological: applying an optimized MnasNet with an advanced single-candidate optimizer to glioma molecular prediction from T2-weighted MRI. The introduction positions the work against prior machine-learning, radiomics, WSI, U-Net, and 3D-CNN approaches, so the gap is reasonably articulated. However, deep-learning radiogenomic prediction of glioma molecular status is already established in cited work, making this an incremental architecture/optimizer extension rather than a field-defining diagnostic advance.

writing_presentation.justification: The paper is understandable in broad outline, but the writing is repetitive and sometimes poorly edited, with generic tutorial passages on CLAHE, augmentation, and optimization that distract from the study. Important presentation problems include inconsistent dataset split descriptions, contradictory metric values between the abstract and comparative results, and a conclusion that repeats background sentences rather than tightly summarizing the study. Figure captions are present but basic, and table captions do not provide enough standalone detail to resolve the methodological ambiguities.

key_strengths: Clinically relevant attempt to predict adult-type diffuse glioma molecular status noninvasively from preoperative T2-weighted MRI.
Uses patient-level splitting and reports multiple classification metrics, with comparisons to several prior approaches.
Includes an ablation-style comparison of original MnasNet, SCO-optimized MnasNet, and the proposed optimized model.
key_concerns: Validation strategy is inconsistent across the abstract, methods, and results, undermining confidence in the reported 97.30% and 92% performance values.
No calibration, uncertainty estimates, power or sample-size rationale, or true prospective external validation is reported.
TRIPOD-relevant reporting is incomplete and no code, model weights, or analyzable dataset are made available in the manuscript.
Writing quality and internal consistency require substantial revision before the scientific claims can be evaluated reliably.
chief_reviewer.rationale: The study has a relevant radiogenomic aim and a plausible technical contribution, but the inconsistent validation description and weak reproducibility posture make the current evidence preliminary. It is most plausible at a lower-tier venue after major methodological and reporting revisions.
